translation: In external contraction of wind-cold, its qi is therefore stuffy, vigorous, and in excess. In internal injury of food, drink, and toil, in both the mouth and nose the qi is short, hurried, and insufficient to reach [full] respiration. How does one divide them? In external contraction of wind-cold, the original qi of the heart and lung is at the outset not yet reduced, and again a pathogen qi is added to assist it, causing the nasal qi to be stuffed, blocked, and not free; the face is red and the passage not open; the qi within the nose cannot come out and all issues from the mouth; but at the utterance of one word, it must be light before and heavy after. Its speech is high, its voice grand, strong, and forceful. In cold damage, then, the nose is dry and without mucus, the face is stuffy and red; its speech is light before and heavy after, its voice grand, strong, and forceful — this is the evidence of excess. In wind damage, then, to be sure, the nose flows clear mucus, its voice is hoarse, its speech sounds as if issuing from within a jar, also light before and heavy after, raised and forceful — this is all evidence of replete and excessive qi. In internal injury of food, drink, and toil, the qi of the heart and lung is first damaged, being wounded by heat; since heat has already wounded the qi, the four limbs have no qi to move, and therefore in both mouth and nose there is shortness of qi and insufficiency of qi, wheezing above, and lazy speech. When people ask something, [the patient] will not answer one of ten; even if against his will he makes forced reply, his qi also is timid, his voice is sunken and low. This is the evidence of shortness, scantiness, and insufficiency of qi. Being so clearly plain, even women and children can distinguish it. How could there be a physician who on the contrary cannot distinguish it?
